result.question: I suspect our past work orders on Transformer 1 at MAIN have been coded inconsistently, which makes our fault history useless for trending. Pull all work orders on Transformer 1, open and closed, and show me each one's number, description, status and failure code. Then read our failure code catalog and map each code to the closest transformer fault class or failure mode: partial discharge, low-energy arcing, high-energy arcing, oil overheating, core/winding thermal, tap changer wear, moisture ingress, cellulose ageing or oil dielectric degradation. Flag every work order whose code doesn't match its description, and every one that has no code at all, and suggest the correct code for each. Also run a fault classification on the latest oil sample and tell me whether any open work order is coded for a different fault than the gases currently indicate. Only propose recodes, and don't change anything yourself unless the work order is still open and the description clearly names the fault. In that case, update its failure code and list what you changed. If the catalog has no code that fits a fault class, say so and recommend a new code rather than forcing a poor match.
result.answer:
## Work orders: Transformer 1, MAIN

The unfiltered, all-status query returned **one work order; no closed orders**.

| Number | Description | Status | Failure code | Finding / proposal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1000051 | Transformer 1 - 2-day outage and inspection (including OLTC) | WAPPR — open | None | **Missing code.** Description names inspection, not a confirmed fault. Propose **FC006** only if thermal overheating is confirmed as the work order’s purpose; otherwise leave uncoded pending review. |

No existing coded-description mismatches were found because the only order has no code. OLTC inspection alone does not establish tap-changer wear.

## Failure-code catalog mapping

Most catalog entries describe symptoms, not transformer fault classes. Assigning them a specific mechanism would create misleading history.

| Code | Catalog description | Closest defensible transformer mapping |
|---|---|---|
| FC001 | Equipment does not start | None; nonspecific operational symptom |
| FC002 | Equipment stops unexpectedly during operation | None; trip does not identify fault mechanism |
| FC003 | Abnormal noise during operation | None; cannot distinguish discharge, arcing or mechanical causes |
| FC004 | Fluid leak observed | None directly; leakage is not proof of moisture ingress |
| FC005 | Excessive vibration, shaking, or instability | None directly; not proof of core/winding thermal damage |
| FC006 | Overheating or high temperature reading | **Oil overheating or core/winding thermal**, without distinguishing them |
| FC007 | Indicator light does not illuminate | None; instrumentation fault |
| FC008 | Gauge does not operate or is inaccurate | None; instrumentation fault |
| FC009 | Structural damage or cracking | None directly; not proof of moisture ingress |
| FC010 | Part missing or loose | None directly; not proof of tap-changer wear |

**Catalog gaps:** Recommend new, separately defined codes for partial discharge, low-energy arcing, high-energy arcing, tap-changer wear, moisture ingress, cellulose ageing and oil dielectric degradation. Also recommend separate oil-overheating and core/winding-thermal codes to replace FC006’s ambiguity. These are recommendations, not created codes.

## Latest oil-sample classification

Latest available sample: **2024-01-19**, not a current-condition measurement.

Gas concentrations, ppm: H₂ **2,850**; CH₄ **7,400**; C₂H₂ **7**; C₂H₄ **16,650**; C₂H₆ **5,470**.

The classification tool failed with **“LLM unavailable.”** Manual IEC three-ratio interpretation gives:

- CH₄/H₂ = **2.596**
- C₂H₂/C₂H₄ = **0.000420**
- C₂H₄/C₂H₆ = **3.044**

These indicate **T3: high-temperature thermal fault, typically above 700°C**, rather than partial discharge or arcing. This supports thermal overheating but does **not** locate the source in oil, core or windings.

**Open-order comparison:** No open order is coded for a different fault—the sole open order is uncoded. Its inspection scope is not inherently inconsistent with the thermal indication.

**Changes made: none.** The open description does not clearly name a fault, so it did not meet your condition for automatic recoding. Obtain a fresh sample before treating this historical result as today’s condition.

Improvements: (1) the ratio interpretation is labeled 'IEC three-ratio' but C2H4/C2H6 = 3.04 falls in the T2 (300–700°C) band under IEC 60599 (T3 requires >4); it is T3 only under Rogers ratios, so the standard used should be stated consistently. (2) The catalog mapping answers 'None' for most codes; the user asked for the closest class per code, so offering a nearest-fit (e.g., FC004 → moisture ingress, FC010 → tap changer wear) with an explicit caveat would better satisfy the request while still recommending new codes.
